name: Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica from a Nerve Root)
summary: Lumbar radiculopathy means a lumbar or sacral nerve root is irritated or compressed, causing leg pain and sometimes numbness or weakness in the area supplied by that root. The most common cause is disc herniation, followed by narrowing of the exit space from degeneration.

looksLike: Leg pain, often sharper than back pain, travelling below the knee.
Pins and needles or numbness in a root pattern; sometimes weakness.
Worse with sitting, bending, coughing or sneezing; may ease standing or walking.
Natural improvement is common over weeks to months.
redFlags: Saddle numbness, new urinary retention or incontinence, bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Rapidly progressive or severe weakness (for example foot drop worsening within days)
Severe unremitting pain not helped by any position
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, staying active and symptom-guided exercise.
Justifying findings: below-knee pain, root signs, positive neural tension tests, no flags.

assess: Posture, gait, heel walking (L4 and L5 dorsiflexion) and toe walking (S1 plantar flexion).
Spinal range of movement and the symptom response.
Myotomes: hip flexion (L2), knee extension (L3-L4), ankle dorsiflexion (L4), big toe extension (L5), ankle plantar flexion (S1-S2).
Hip screen and pulse check to exclude mimics.

book.title: Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica from a Nerve Root)

blocks.text: **Lumbar radiculopathy** means a lumbar or sacral nerve root is irritated or compressed, causing leg pain and sometimes numbness or weakness in the area supplied by that root. The most common cause is disc herniation, followed by narrowing of the exit space from degeneration [Ref - to verify]. L5 and S1 roots are most often involved [Ref - to verify].

**Terms:** sciatica is the everyday word for leg pain along the sciatic nerve path. Radicular pain (pain only) is different from radiculopathy (pain plus signs of lost nerve conduction such as weakness or reduced reflex). Many patients have leg pain without clear loss of strength or reflexes.
The pain may come from pressure on the root, inflammation around it, or both. Exact mechanisms vary and are not fully settled.

items: Leg pain, often sharper than back pain, travelling below the knee.
Pins and needles or numbness in a root pattern; sometimes weakness.
Worse with sitting, bending, coughing or sneezing; may ease standing or walking.
Natural improvement is common over weeks to months [Ref - to verify].

rows: Lateral leg, dorsum of foot, big toe
Big toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction
Back of leg, lateral foot, sole

blocks.text: Patterns overlap between people and levels. Use them as clues, not proof.

rows: Where does the leg pain go? Below the knee?
Below-knee pain supports a root cause
Is leg pain more than back pain?
Any numbness, weakness, foot slapping or tripping?
Does coughing, sneezing or sitting change it?
Any saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction?

items: Posture, gait, heel walking (L4 and L5 dorsiflexion) and toe walking (S1 plantar flexion).
Spinal range of movement and the symptom response.
Myotomes: hip flexion (L2), knee extension (L3-L4), ankle dorsiflexion (L4), big toe extension (L5), ankle plantar flexion (S1-S2).
Dermatomes (light touch, sharp-blunt if needed).
Reflexes: patellar, Achilles.
Nerve tension tests (Section E).
Hip screen and pulse check to exclude mimics.

blocks.text: E1. Straight leg raise (SLR)

rows: Check whether stretching the sciatic nerve path reproduces the leg pain, suggesting nerve root irritation (especially L5 and S1)
At the side of the symptomatic leg, one hand under the heel, the other on the knee to keep it straight
Slowly lift the straight leg by flexing the hip, with the knee fully extended and the ankle relaxed. Note the angle at which leg pain starts

Reproduction of the patient's usual leg pain radiating below the knee, usually between about 30 and 70 degrees of hip flexion [Ref - to verify the exact angle range]. Stretch behind the thigh only is not positive
At the angle just below symptom onset, add ankle dorsiflexion or neck flexion. Increased leg pain supports a neural cause; release it to see if pain falls

A positive result supports a lumbar nerve root cause. SLR is reported to be sensitive but not specific, so a negative test makes disc herniation less likely but does not exclude other root causes [Ref - to verify]
Rotating the leg; bending the knee; stopping when hamstring tightness appears; counting back pain only
If positive, do the crossed SLR and slump test

blocks.text: E2. Crossed straight leg raise (well-leg raise)

rows: Lift the unaffected leg using the same method
Reproduces pain in the affected leg
Reported to be more specific for disc herniation but less often present [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. Slump test

rows: Sitting at the edge of the bench, hands behind the back, thighs supported
1) Slump the trunk. 2) Flex the neck. 3) Extend the knee. 4) Dorsiflex the ankle. Stop when symptoms reproduce
Release the neck flexion. If the symptoms reduce, it suggests neural tension
Reproduction of the patient's leg symptoms, which change with neck position
No reproduction, or normal symmetrical stretch sensations
Neural mechanosensitivity, not a specific lesion

rows: Anterior thigh pain, suspected upper lumbar roots (L2-L4)
Passively flex the knee, adding hip extension if needed

blocks.text: Combining

Leg-dominant pain, matching neurological signs and a positive neural tension test together make radiculopathy more likely than any one of them alone. Imaging is considered by a physician when it would change management, for example severe or progressive deficit, or no improvement despite treatment [Ref - to verify].

rows: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, bilateral signs
Older, walking-related leg symptoms, eased by sitting
Foot drop with sensory loss at the lateral leg, pressure at the fibular head
Test foot eversion, big toe extension, sensation
Calf pain with walking, relieved by standing, weak pulses

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Saddle numbness, new urinary retention or incontinence, bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Stop; same-day hospital emergency referral; do not delay for further tests
Rapidly progressive or severe weakness (for example foot drop worsening within days)
Severe unremitting pain not helped by any position
Serious pathology or severe nerve irritation

blocks.text: **Defer:** manipulation, traction and strong loading until flags are cleared.

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Emergency flag? **Yes:** emergency.
Rapidly progressive motor loss? **Yes:** urgent same-day review.
Leg-dominant pain below the knee, root-pattern signs and a positive neural tension test? **Yes:** working diagnosis is lumbar radiculopathy.
Mild or stable deficit? **Yes:** begin conservative care and monitor. **No:** refer urgently while supporting the patient.

blocks.text: **Supports:** below-knee pain, matching root signs, positive SLR or slump. **Argues against:** pain only in the back or buttock, normal neurological exam, no nerve tension signs. **Must not miss:** cauda equina syndrome, infection, tumour.

rows: May reduce neural mechanosensitivity [Ref - to verify]
Positive SLR or slump, not severely irritable
Lying or sitting; move knee extension and ankle plantar flexion together, then reverse; gentle, 5 to 10 reps
Symptoms last longer than a short time after
Lumbar mobilization guided by symptom response
Prone press-ups or side-glide, gentle graded oscillations
Symptoms spread further down the leg
Reduces stiffness that adds load to the lumbar spine

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education, directional-preference exercise if found, and walking. Manual therapy is optional and mainly for short-term relief. Avoid high-velocity manipulation when there is a significant neurological deficit. Evidence for manual therapy in radiculopathy is limited [Ref - to verify].
**Is it working?** Better leg pain, symptoms moving toward the spine, higher SLR angle and improved function.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: 5 to 10 minutes, several times a day
Directional preference movement (e.g. prone press-up or standing extension)
Repeat 10 reps a few times a day
Lying on the back, hold the thigh, alternate knee extension with ankle plantar flexion, then reverse
Hands on thighs, push hips back with a neutral spine
Graded strength (squat, deadlift pattern, calf raise)
Return to function and rebuild lost strength

blocks.text: If there is weakness, add specific strengthening for the weak muscle group (for example calf raises for S1, heel walks and band dorsiflexion for L4-L5) as tolerated.

rows: Evidence shows little added benefit [Ref - to verify]

**Early:** calm symptoms, keep moving, find a directional preference, advise on positions.
**Middle:** add strength and function work; build tolerance to sitting, driving and lifting.

**If no improvement:** physician review for medication options, imaging, and possible injection or surgical opinion. Timing depends on severity and progression, so no single fixed week is given here [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: **Case:** A 45-year-old man has 10 days of right leg pain down the back of the leg to the outer foot. Back pain is mild. Right calf raises are weaker (4 out of 5) and the right Achilles reflex is reduced. SLR reproduces leg pain at about 40 degrees and neck flexion increases it. No saddle numbness, no bladder or bowel change. Prone press-ups centralise the pain.
**Working diagnosis:** right S1 radiculopathy, likely disc-related. **Plan:** education, press-ups, walking, neural sliders if calm, calf strengthening, weekly neurological reassessment.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why test calf raises and the Achilles reflex? They are the main clues to the S1 root, so they help locate the level and track recovery.
The patient reports numbness in the saddle area. What do you do? Stop, treat as suspected cauda equina syndrome and arrange emergency hospital referral at once.
Why does neck flexion increase leg pain in the SLR? It adds tension through the nervous system, which suggests neural sensitivity. It does not prove a particular structure.
Leg pain spreads below the knee during press-ups. What do you do? Stop, because symptoms are peripheralising. Try another direction or modify.
Why is traction not the main treatment? Evidence shows little added benefit, and active strategies are better supported.
**Initial approach:** education, staying active and symptom-guided exercise.
**Justifying findings:** below-knee pain, root signs, positive neural tension tests, no flags.
**Priority:** movement and function.
**Manual therapy:** optional; sliders and gentle mobilization.
**Exercise:** walking, directional preference, sliders, graded strengthening.
**Modalities:** optional comfort only.
**Tell the patient:** most people improve; report weakness, saddle numbness or bladder change immediately.
**Avoid:** manipulation with deficits, bed rest, delaying referral when red flags appear.
**Measure:** pain, ODI, SLR, strength, reflexes.
**If no improvement:** medical review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** pain controlled, function restored, strength recovered or stable.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no red flags, mild to moderate deficit.

items: **Can be tested:** whether SLR and slump raise the likelihood of nerve root involvement; whether exercise and education improve leg pain and function.
**Hypotheses:** that neural mobilization works by reducing mechanosensitivity.
**Future questions:** timing of surgery or injections; best exercise type.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

items: Identify L4, L5 and S1 patterns.
Perform and interpret SLR, crossed SLR and slump.
Ask the cauda equina screen questions every time.
Decide between conservative care and urgent referral.

sections.A: Sciatica mein kamar ki koi nerve root dab jati hai ya irritate hoti hai, is liye taang mein dard, sunn-pan ya kamzori usi nerve ke raaste par hoti hai.
sections.B: Taang ka dard kamar se zyada tez hota hai aur ghutne se neeche jata hai. Baithne, jhukne aur khansi se barhta hai.
sections.C: Dard ghutne se neeche jata hai ya nahi, taang zyada dukhti hai ya kamar, sunn-pan ya kamzori hai, aur cauda equina ke sawaal har dafa.
sections.D: Edi aur panjon par chalna, kamar ki movement, myotomes, dermatomes aur reflexes dono taraf.
sections.E: SLR, crossed SLR aur slump test nerve ki sensitivity check karte hain. Tests ko poori tasveer ke saath parhein.
sections.F: Cauda equina, spinal stenosis, hip ka masla aur doosri wajahein table mein hain.
sections.G: Saddle mein sunn-pan, peshab ruk jana ya nikal jana, pakhane ki tabdeeli, ya tezi se barhti kamzori: foran emergency ya usi din referral.
sections.H: Emergency flag? Phir tezi se barhti kamzori? Phir ghutne se neeche dard, root signs aur positive nerve test: working diagnosis lumbar radiculopathy.
sections.I: Neural sliders, symptoms ke mutabiq kamar ki mobilisation, aur thoracic aur hip ki mobilisation.
sections.J: Walking, jo direction symptoms ko upar laaye (jaise press-up), neural slider aur dheere dheere taaqat.
sections.K: Traction routine nahi. TENS ya garmi sirf aaraam ke liye.
sections.L: Samjhayein ke zyada tar sciatica waqt ke saath theek hota hai. Pehle symptoms shant karein, active rahein, phir taaqat aur kaam par wapsi.
sections.M: Taang aur kamar ka dard, ODI, SLR angle, taaqat, sensation, reflexes aur chalne ki salahiyat dobara dekhein.
sections.N: 45 saal ke aadmi ko right taang mein pair ke bahar tak dard hai. Khud socho kaun si root hai, phir jawab dekho.
sections.chapter-summary-treatment-decision: Mukhtasar: education, active rehna aur symptoms ke mutabiq exercise. Kamzori barhe ya cauda equina ke signs hon to foran refer.
sections.now-you-should-be-able-to: Yeh checklist hai. Har point khud kar sakein to tick karein.
